turns.t: Hi. Um, I think I might have malaria. I got back from Ghana ten days ago, and I've been getting these fevers.
Thank you for coming promptly. Tell me about the fevers.
They come in waves. I'll be fine, then I get cold and shivering, and then burning hot, and drenched in sweat. It's every second day, I think.
How long does each episode last?
Five or six hours. Then I'm wiped out.
Did you take malaria tablets on the trip? ~
I took them for the first week, and then I stopped. I felt sick on them. ~
That's useful to know. Any diarrhoea or vomiting?
No. No diarrhoea. I was a bit nauseous during the fevers, but I haven't been sick.
Any rash, or yellowing of your skin or eyes?
No rash. No yellow.
Any breathing problems, or cough?
No, nothing like that. My chest is fine.
Any medical conditions?
Asthma, mild, I use a blue inhaler occasionally.
Let me examine you. Lie back. ~
Okay.
Your tummy is soft, and I can feel your spleen edge, it's a little bit enlarged.
Is that bad? ~
It's what happens with malaria, so I'm taking it seriously. From what you describe, fevers every second day after a trip to West Africa, I'd say malaria is the likely cause until proven otherwise.
Oh God. Is it dangerous? ~
It can be, if it's left, and the most serious type can get bad quickly. But it's very treatable when caught early. ~
What happens now? ~
I'm sending you straight to the hospital this afternoon, and I want a malaria blood film done today. I'll ring ahead.
Today? Right. ~
Yes, today. They'll test your blood and probably start treatment straight away if it's positive. ~
Can I drive myself? ~
I'd rather you didn't. Is there someone who can take you? ~
My flatmate. ~
Please call them now. If you become confused, very drowsy, vomit repeatedly, or get a severe headache on the way, call 999.
Okay. Okay, thank you, doctor. ~
You did the right thing. Go straight there. ~
